highlight.text: But he was also a specialist in horse-painting and followed in this respect very closely Han Kan and Li Lung-mien. In fact, he considered himself fully equal to the latter

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: A History of Early Chinese Painting, vol. II

source.label: Palace Museum record (via Wikidata): 人骑图卷, a handscroll 620 cm long with its colophons

work.text: From my early days I liked to paint horses, and I thought that I knew completely their character. … as to the comparison with Li Lung-mien, I have no objection and may well be equal to him.

source.author: Zhao Mengfu (Chao Meng-fu)
source.title: Inscription on a horse painting
source.publisher: translated in Osvald Sirén, A History of Early Chinese Painting, vol. II (The Medici Society, 1933; Internet Archive scan)

work.text: He was known for his paintings of horses.

moment.text: Chao Meng-fu found in the work of a T’ang dynasty artist a theme concerning horses, which was especially fitted to his own time when the Mongol passion for horses had been imitated throughout China.

source.author: John C. Ferguson
source.title: Chinese Painting
source.publisher: University of Chicago Press (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: It seems furthermore that Chao Meng-fu did not paint horses simply as motives of animal life, but represented them also in a symbolic sense.

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: A History of Early Chinese Painting, vol. II
